summary:
MarsWalk is a traverse planner for astronauts walking on Mars in suits. Every step out is a step the crew must walk back on limited oxygen, yet today's maps show where things are, not whether you can still make it home. MarsWalk answers that question for every metre and minute of a walk.
It reads the ground the way a boot would, using NASA data: 1 m HiRISE stereo terrain and imagery, THEMIS thermal inertia for loose sand, Curiosity RAD radiation and live DONKI space weather. It marks ground too steep or rough to walk, finds the route through the science stops that costs the least oxygen, and shades a safe zone showing where the crew can still turn back with the 30% reserve intact. Every plan is checked for slope, oxygen, radio line of sight to the rover, time to shelter from a solar storm and terrain uncertainty, and the cautions are shown, not hidden.
The crew can ask questions out loud, read the next stop and turn-back time on an e-ink suit display, and rehearse the route in a 3-D simulator on Gale crater's real terrain. MarsWalk plans at Gale and any usable HiRISE stereo site on Mars.
details:
Every step out is a step you have to walk back. On Mars, a suited crew leaves the rover with 8 hours of oxygen and keeps 30% of it for the walk home. A hiker on Earth who misjudges the way back gets tired. An astronaut who misjudges it runs out of air. Maps show where things are. MarsWalk shows whether you can still get home, from every metre of the walk and at every minute of the day.

What it does

  1. Reads the ground the way a boot would. From NASA's 1 m HiRISE stereo terrain it measures slope over 1 m and 5 m and roughness, and THEMIS thermal inertia flags loose sand. Ground steeper than 25° over 5 m or 35° over 1 m, or rougher than 0.8 m, is off limits.
  2. Finds the cheapest walk in oxygen, not metres. It searches every metre of the grid using the walking model of NASA's SEXTANT traverse planner. On a 10° climb a suited walker draws less power but spends 3.3 times more energy per metre, so routes bend around hills.
  3. Plans the day. Five science stops on Curiosity's Mount Sharp boxwork: 1.71 km, 3 h 31 min outside, 63% of the usable oxygen, and 2 h 05 min to spare.
  4. Shows where you can still go. Slide the clock and a green safe zone shrinks: everywhere the crew can still turn back with the reserve untouched.
  5. Checks the plan before anyone steps out. Steepest step 17° (limit 20°). Space weather from NASA DONKI. Storm shelter: from anywhere on the route the walk home is under 15 minutes, inside the 30 minutes a solar particle storm may give. The two cautions are shown to the crew, not hidden: 16 minutes with no radio line of sight to the rover, and 30 m of ground that could be off limits within the terrain's 0.3 m error.
  6. Answers out loud. Ask "How far is S3?" and it answers 730 m on foot, about 28 minutes. Every number comes from the planner itself, not from an AI model.
  7. Goes on the suit. A 7.5-inch e-ink display on an ESP32 shows the next stop, oxygen left and when to turn back, like car navigation.
  8. Lets you rehearse it. A 3-D simulator puts you on Gale's real 1 m ground at Mars gravity, under the Sun where it will really be that morning. It moves you with the same physics as the planner, step for step. There is also a hidden skateboard. On Martian dirt, it barely rolls.
  9. Works beyond Gale. Click anywhere NASA has a 1 m HiRISE stereo terrain model (843 usable of 1,370, about 0.1% of Mars) and MarsWalk finds the data in NASA's archive, downloads it, lines it up with the map and plans there with the same code. We tested it at Jezero crater.

Benefits and impact. EVA planners get a plan whose safety margins are visible, not buried in a spreadsheet. The crew carries the same numbers on the suit and can ask for them out loud. Mission designers can compare landing sites by how far a crew could safely walk. Everything runs on public NASA data and the code is open, so a real suit's numbers drop into one config file.

Why it is creative. It treats the walk home, not the destination, as the answer. It plans for oxygen instead of distance. And one model drives everything: the map, the voice answers, the suit display and the simulator, checked against each other by tests.

What we weighed.

  • Accuracy: we found the HiRISE terrain sat 45 m off NASA's base map (33.5 m south, 30.5 m east), measured it and corrected it.
  • Honesty about limits: it cannot see rocks smaller than 2 to 3 m, or sand inside the boxwork hollows. Away from Gale, radiation is estimated from Gale's Curiosity measurements scaled by air pressure.
  • Assumptions you can change: suit limits live in a config file, not in code.
  • Testing: 120 automated tests check the models against published values, including NASA's Mars24 Sun examples and Curiosity's sol numbers.

Tools. Python (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, numba, rasterio/GDAL, pyproj, SQLAlchemy), TypeScript and React with OpenLayers for the map and Three.js for the simulator, Vite, an ESP32 with a 7.5-inch e-ink panel (C++, GxEPD2), Vercel hosting, Supabase (the Postgres store we are moving saved plans and Bases into) and GitHub.

Use of AI. We used AI assistants (Claude and Cursor) for brainstorming, research, coding, debugging, data analysis and the presentation. Every number in the app comes from NASA data and published models, and the tests check them. No images are AI-generated: every picture is a screenshot of the running app on NASA imagery.

NASA Mars Trek: Curiosity HiRISE and CTX mosaics, THEMIS daytime infrared
THEMIS global thermal inertia mosaic (Mars Odyssey)
NASA DONKI space weather: CMEs, WSA-ENLIL arrivals, solar energetic particles, flares
Curiosity rover location map (waypoints for the five stops)
Curiosity RAD surface radiation (Hassler et al. 2014, Science)
NASA GISS Mars24 Sunclock algorithm (Sun position and Mars time)
